intro.html: Some things happen because people plan them; others happen by chance. English has a whole family of words for chance, from happy surprises to small accidents to full-scale disasters.

Chance itself: fortuitous, happenstance, fluke. Good luck: serendipity (lucky finds), windfall (unexpected gain), propitious (favorable signs). Bad luck: hapless (unlucky), mishap (a small accident), calamity (a disaster), debacle (a total failure).
Look for the old word hap, which meant luck or chance: it hides in happen, happy, perhaps, hapless, mishap and happenstance.

words.def: happening by chance, often by lucky chance
words.ex: Our meeting at the airport was {fortuitous}: neither of us knew the other was flying that day.
words.ctx: The discovery was {fortuitous} rather than planned; the scientist had been studying something else entirely when she noticed the strange glow in her dish.
words.etym: From Latin fortuitus, “happening by chance,” from fors (chance).
words.note: Fortuitous first meant only “by chance,” lucky or not. Today it often means “happening by lucky chance,” and dictionaries accept both.

mn.text: Caught in the rain, Lila ducks under a shop awning and finds her old best friend sheltering there too; the meeting, pure chance and good fortune, is {fortuitous}.

scene.alt: Two old friends who met by chance in the rain hug under an umbrella.

words.def: the luck of finding good things without looking for them
words.ex: By pure {serendipity}, Sami found his favorite book at a yard sale for a dime.
words.ctx: Searching the attic for a flashlight, Grandma found her mother’s long-lost diary instead; she called it {serendipity}, since she had given up hope of ever seeing it again.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: Coined in 1754 from Serendip, an old name for Sri Lanka, after a Persian fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept finding things they were not looking for.

mn.cue: a SERENE DIP finds a treasure
mn.text: Taking a serene dip in the lake, Omar feels something under his toes: a lost gold ring. Finding something wonderful without looking for it is {serendipity}.

scene.alt: A man wading at the beach holds up a gold ring he found by chance under his toes.

words.def: favorable; likely to lead to success
words.ex: Clear skies and a steady breeze made it a {propitious} day for the kite festival.
words.ctx: With customers lining up out the door every morning, the owners decided it was a {propitious} moment to open a second bakery across town.

mn.cue: a PRO-FISH day: every sign says GO
mn.text: The old fisherman sees calm water, a rainbow and fish leaping all around his boat; every sign is good, so it is a {propitious} day to fish.

scene.alt: A happy fisherman in a rowboat points at leaping fish under a rainbow.

words.def: a lucky or unlikely chance happening
words.ex: Her first basket from half court was a {fluke}; she missed the next twenty.
words.ctx: Some called the underdogs’ win a {fluke}, but when the team won its next three games as well, the doubters went quiet.
words.note: A fluke is also a kind of flatfish and one of the two halves of a whale’s tail; the “lucky chance” fluke is a separate word.

mn.text: Pip tosses a paper ball over his shoulder without even looking, and it flies straight into the trash can across the room; a lucky shot like that is a {fluke}.

scene.alt: A boy is amazed as a paper ball he tossed without looking flies into a far-off trash can.

words.ex: By {happenstance}, the two cousins ended up in the same college dorm.
words.ctx: Their friendship began through {happenstance}, not planning: both had grabbed the same umbrella from the lost-and-found box on the same rainy afternoon.
words.etym: A blend of happen and circumstance.

mn.text: Two strangers reach for the very last loaf of bread at the same moment and end up sharing a picnic; their meeting just happened, by {happenstance}.

scene.alt: A man and a woman reach for the same last loaf of bread at the same moment and laugh.

words.def: an unexpected gain, such as money one did not work for
words.ex: A {windfall} from a forgotten savings account paid for the family’s trip to the coast.
words.ctx: The town had no money for a new library; the funds came as a {windfall} when a dusty painting in the town hall attic turned out to be worth a fortune.
words.etym: First meant fruit or trees blown down by the wind, free for anyone to gather.

mn.cue: the WIND makes the fruit FALL
mn.text: A gust of wind shakes the old tree, and a dozen ripe pieces of fruit tumble right into Ivy’s basket; a gift you did not work for is a {windfall}.

scene.alt: Wind blows fruit off a tree, and it falls straight into a delighted girl’s basket.

words.def: unlucky; having one bad break after another
words.ex: The {hapless} hiker lost his map, then his hat, then his left boot.
words.ctx: The {hapless} goalie had a miserable afternoon: the sun was in his eyes, his glove tore, and the winning goal bounced in off his own knee.
words.etym: From Middle English hap (luck) + -less: without luck.

mn.text: Poor Felix: a crow steals his sandwich, a rain cloud follows only him, and his umbrella turns inside out. With no luck at all, he is {hapless}.

scene.alt: A rain cloud pours on a sad man while a crow flies off with his sandwich.

words.def: a disaster that causes great loss or suffering
words.ex: The flood was the worst {calamity} the valley had seen in a hundred years.
words.ctx: What began as a small kitchen fire became a {calamity}: the flames spread down the whole block, and dozens of families lost their homes.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

mn.cue: no CALM at all: a disaster
mn.text: A giant wave sweeps away the whole sandcastle city the children spent all day building; to them, it is a {calamity}.

scene.alt: Two children panic as a huge wave crashes over the sandcastle city they built.

words.def: a small accident or bit of bad luck
words.ex: Apart from one {mishap} with a spilled paint can, the mural went up without trouble.
words.ctx: The camping trip had only one {mishap}: a raccoon stole our pancakes, but nobody was hurt, and we laughed about it for weeks.
words.etym: From Middle English: mis- (bad) + hap (chance), the same hap found in happen and perhaps.

mn.cue: MIS + HAP: a little BAD LUCK
mn.text: Ivy trips, and her ice cream cone lands upside down on the dog’s head; it is only a small {mishap}, and the dog does not mind one bit.

scene.alt: A girl trips and her ice cream lands on a happy dog’s head.

words.ex: The school play was a {debacle}: the curtain fell, the lights went out and the lead forgot every line.
words.ctx: The new phone’s launch was a {debacle}; the batteries overheated, the stores ran out of chargers, and the company had to take back every phone within a week.
words.etym: From French débâcle, the breaking up of ice on a river, from débâcler (to unbolt, to set free).

mn.cue: de-BAKE-le: the bake-off that fell apart
mn.text: At the big bake-off, Nell’s tower cake wobbles, tilts and crashes onto the judges’ table; the whole entry is a {debacle}.

scene.alt: A baker panics as her tall cake topples onto the judge’s table.

after.cap: Chance, good luck and bad luck.

after.html: The old word hap (luck) explains three of these words: hapless is luck-less, a mishap is bad luck, and happenstance is what just happens.

items.why: False. Hapless means unlucky: hap (luck) + -less (without). A hapless person may be quite capable, just unlucky.
Fortuitous first meant by chance, lucky or not; today it is also used to mean happening by lucky chance.

items.q: Looking for her keys in the couch, Rosa found a twenty-dollar bill she had lost a year ago. This is…
items.why: Finding something good that you were not looking for is serendipity.

items.q: The family received an unexpected check for five hundred dollars. It was a…
items.why: A windfall is an unexpected gain, like fruit blown down by the wind.
